findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed after successful use
findings.body: When the recovery-codes credential lives in a federated user storage, validation goes through user.credentialManager().isValid(...), which delegates to the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid(). Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (which removes the used code from the stored credential as part of isValid), a federated storage has no update hook here, so the used code remains valid forever. Consequences: the same recovery code can be replayed indefinitely, getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() always returns the first code, and allCodesUsed() never becomes true, so the cleanup/re-enrollment logic below never triggers for federated users. The PR's own test storage (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) demonstrates this: it only checks membership in the stored list without removing the used code.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById cannot remove a federated recovery-codes credential
findings.body: When all codes are used, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). For a credential that was found via getFederatedCredentialsStream() (the new RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential path), removeStoredCredentialById only operates on the local store, so the federated credential is never deleted. The storage would need disableCredentialType/updateCredential semantics instead; as written the exhausted credential silently persists in the user storage.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes sent to user storage while local storage hashes them
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the plaintext generatedCodes list into the UserCredentialModel challenge response sent to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Any user storage implementing CredentialInputUpdater will therefore persist the raw recovery codes, whereas the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider stores only hashed codes. This creates an inconsistent security posture (plaintext recovery codes in external stores) with no documentation or warning to storage implementers that they are expected to hash/protect the value themselves.
